sentences.text: Polacanthus was a dinosaur covered in protective armor plates and sharp spikes.
The only known species is Polacanthus foxii, a nodosaurid thyreophoran that grew to a length between four and five meters.
The holotype, which serves as the specimen the species is based on, is an incomplete skeleton missing the head, neck, front armor, and rear legs.
The name Polacanthus comes from Greek words meaning many and spine, describing the creature's many spines.
A 2020 review of British ankylosaur fossils found that no other specimens could be confidently linked to this genus, leaving only the original type specimen.
Reverend William Fox discovered the type species on the Isle of Wight in early 1865 at a location called Barnes High on the southwest coast.
Fox reported the find in a lecture to the British Association in September 1865 and permitted Richard Owen to name the dinosaur Polacanthus foxii.
A second known specimen was later found and excavated by Dr. William T. Blows in 1979.
Darren Naish and David Martill estimated the length at five meters in 2001, and Gregory S. Paul supported this length estimate in 2010 while suggesting a body mass of two tons.
Thomas Holtz provided a lower size estimation in 2012, suggesting a length of four meters and a mass between 227 and 454 kilograms.
Polacanthus belongs to the class Ornithischia, and its parent group is the family Nodosauridae.
Fox assigned Polacanthus to Dinosauria in 1865, while Huxley and Hulke later assigned it to Scelidosauridae.
In 1978, Coombs placed Polacanthus in the family Nodosauridae within the suborder Ankylosauria.

In 1996, a species named Polacanthus rudgwickensis was described based on fragmentary fossils previously misidentified as Iguanodon, but in 2015 it was reclassified into the separate genus Horshamosaurus.
Polacanthus was an extinct genus of ankylosaurian dinosaurs that lived in England during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago.
Polacanthus lived during the Barremian age, approximately 124 to 132 million years ago.
It is debated whether Polacanthus is a basal member of the family Nodosauridae or belongs to a separate family called Polacanthidae.
Researchers suggest that the genus Polacanthoides may be a chimera because its component bones likely belonged to Polacanthus.
It has been suggested that Polacanthus is identical to Hylaeosaurus armatus, but this was rejected by Blows in 1987 due to differences in age and anatomy.
